chem_ocrb.1.8.summary: Mastering chemical formulae and balanced equations is essential for quantitative chemistry in OCR GCSE Chemistry B. This section covers writing accurate formulae for elements and ionic compounds using common ions, applying the cross-over method, and constructing fully balanced symbol equations including state symbols. Grade 9 success requires careful tracking of charges, handling polyatomic ions with brackets, and obeying the law of conservation of mass across all reactions.

core.h: Introduction to Chemical Formulae and Elements
core.p: A chemical formula uses chemical symbols from the Periodic Table to show the relative number of atoms of each element in a substance. Elements exist either as single atoms (monatomic, like noble gases) or as molecules containing fixed numbers of covalently bonded atoms.
bullets: Monatomic elements consist of unbonded single atoms, such as Helium (He) and Neon (Ne).

Diatomic elements always exist as molecules containing two atoms covalently bonded together, such as Hydrogen (H2), Nitrogen (N2), Oxygen (O2), Fluorine (F2), Chlorine (Cl2), Bromine (Br2), and Iodine (I2).
Allotrope structures like carbon can be written simply by their element symbol if giant (C for graphite/diamond) or as specific molecules (O3 for ozone).
The formula of a compound tells you the exact ratio of different elements combined within it.

callouts.p: Memorise the seven diatomic elements: H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2, and I2. They are never written as single letters in equations unless reacting as individual atoms.

core.h: Common Positive Ions (Cations)
core.p: Cations are positively charged ions formed when metal atoms (or hydrogen) lose electrons. In ionic compounds, metals form positive ions corresponding to their group number, with a few crucial transition metal exceptions.
bullets: Group 1 metals lose one electron to form 1+ ions: Lithium (Li+), Sodium (Na+), Potassium (K+).
Group 2 metals lose two electrons to form 2+ ions: Magnesium (Mg2+), Calcium (Ca2+), Barium (Ba2+).
Group 3 metals (like Aluminium) lose three electrons to form Aluminium (Al3+).
Transition metals can form multiple ions denoted by Roman numerals: Iron(II) (Fe2+), Iron(III) (Fe3+), Copper(II) (Cu2+).
Special non-metal cation: Hydrogen (H+) and Ammonium (NH4+).

callouts.p: A positively charged ion formed by the loss of electrons from an atom or group of atoms.

core.h: Common Negative Ions (Anions)
core.p: Anions are negatively charged ions formed when non-metal atoms gain electrons. They include simple monatomic ions from Groups 6 and 7, as well as complex polyatomic ions containing oxygen.
bullets: Group 7 elements gain one electron to form 1- halide ions: Fluoride (F-), Chloride (Cl-), Bromide (Br-), Iodide (I-).
Group 6 elements gain two electrons to form 2- ions: Oxide (O2-), Sulfide (S2-).
Hydroxide ion is a key 1- polyatomic ion: OH-.
Sulfates, carbonates, and nitrates are essential polyatomic anions: Sulfate (SO4 2-), Carbonate (CO3 2-), Nitrate (NO3 -).

callouts.p: Polyatomic ions are groups of covalently bonded atoms that carry an overall electrical charge. Treat the whole unit as a single entity when balancing charges.

core.h: Deriving Formulae Using the Cross-Over Method
core.p: Because ionic compounds are electrically neutral overall, the total positive charge from cations must exactly balance the total negative charge from anions. The cross-over method is a foolproof way to find the empirical formula.
bullets: Step 1: Write down the symbols and charges of the positive ion and negative ion side by side.
Step 2: Ignore the positive and negative signs, and cross the numbers over to become the subscript of the opposite ion.
Step 3: Simplify the ratio of subscripts if they share a common factor (e.g., Mg2+ and O2- becomes Mg2O2, which simplifies to MgO).
Step 4: If a polyatomic ion needs a subscript greater than 1, enclose its formula in brackets before writing the subscript outside (e.g., Ca2+ and OH- becomes Ca(OH)2).

callouts.p: Never change the internal numbers inside a polyatomic ion formula (e.g., NO3 remains NO3). If you need two nitrates, write (NO3)2, never N2O6.

core.h: Introduction to Balanced Equations
core.p: Chemical reactions rearrange atoms, but no atoms are created or destroyed. This is the Law of Conservation of Mass. A balanced symbol equation ensures that the number of atoms of each element is identical on both the reactant and product sides.
bullets: Reactants are written on the left-hand side of the equation, separated by plus signs.
Products are written on the right-hand side, separated from reactants by an arrow (-> meaning 'react to form').
Large numbers placed in front of chemical formulas are called stoichiometric coefficients. They multiply every atom in that formula.
Small subscript numbers inside formulas must never be changed when balancing an equation, as doing so changes the chemical substance itself.

callouts.p: Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products in a chemical reaction because atoms are only rearranged, not created or destroyed.

core.h: Step-by-Step Balancing of Equations
core.p: Balancing equations requires a systematic, methodical approach. Work through elements one by one, typically leaving hydrogen and oxygen until the end because they appear frequently in multiple compounds.
bullets: Step 1: Write the unbalanced word equation, then convert it into a correct symbol equation using accurate formulae.
Step 2: Count the number of atoms of each element on both sides of the equation.
Step 3: Balance elements that appear in only one reactant and one product first by inserting coefficients.
Step 4: Balance hydrogen and oxygen atoms last.
Step 5: Re-check all atom counts on both sides to ensure complete balance.

callouts.p: Keep a running tally table of atom counts underneath your working out during an exam to avoid silly arithmetic errors.

core.h: State Symbols in Equations
core.p: State symbols provide vital physical information about the state of matter of each reactant and product under reaction conditions. They are written in parentheses immediately after each chemical formula.
bullets: (s) stands for solid - substances that are solid at room temperature and pressure.
(l) stands for liquid - pure liquid substances, most notably water (H2O(l)).
(g) stands for gas - substances that exist as gases at room temperature and pressure.
(aq) stands for aqueous - meaning the substance is dissolved in water to form an aqueous solution.

callouts.p: Do not confuse (l) and (aq). (l) is for a pure molten or liquid substance like liquid bromine or water. (aq) is strictly for a solute dissolved in water, like salt water or hydrochloric acid.

core.h: Ionic Equations for Reactions in Solution
core.p: When ionic compounds dissolve in water, they dissociate into mobile ions. Ionic equations strip out spectator ions—ions that do not take part in the chemical reaction—to focus purely on the species that change.
bullets: Start with a fully balanced symbol equation including state symbols.
Split all aqueous ionic substances into their respective constituent ions (e.g., HCl(aq) becomes H+(aq) + Cl-(aq)).
Solids (s), liquids (l), and gases (g) are never split into ions because they are not dissociated.
Cancel out identical ions that appear on both sides of the equation (spectator ions).
Rewrite the remaining ions and species to form the final ionic equation.

callouts.p: Spectator ions remain unchanged throughout the reaction. Omitting them highlights the core chemical change, such as H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l) in neutralisation.

fig.cap: Visual breakdown of splitting aqueous species into ions for an ionic equation.

core.h: Higher Tier: Half Equations for Electrolysis
core.p: At Higher tier, students must write half equations for reactions occurring at electrodes during electrolysis. Half equations show explicitly how electrons are gained or lost by ions.
bullets: Reduction half equations show electrons being gained by positive ions at the cathode (e.g., Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu).
Oxidation half equations show electrons being lost by negative ions at the anode (e.g., 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-).
The number of electrons gained in reduction must equal the number of electrons lost in oxidation when combining half equations.
Always include state symbols in half equations (e.g., aqueous ions becoming solid metals or gases).

callouts.p: An equation that describes reduction (gain of electrons) or oxidation (loss of electrons) at an individual electrode.

core.h: Common Acids and Their Formulae
core.p: Acids are hydrogen-containing compounds that produce hydrogen ions (H+) when dissolved in water. Knowing their exact chemical formulae is mandatory for writing neutralisation and titration equations.
bullets: Hydrochloric acid: HCl(aq)
Sulfuric acid: H2SO4(aq)
Nitric acid: HNO3(aq)
Phosphoric acid (Triple only extension): H3PO4(aq)

callouts.p: Sulfuric acid is diprotic (provides two H+ ions per molecule, hence H2SO4), whereas hydrochloric acid is monoprotic (HCl).

core.h: Precipitation Reactions and Formulae
core.p: Precipitation occurs when two soluble salt solutions are mixed, producing an insoluble solid product known as a precipitate. Writing equations for these requires correct solubility predictions.
bullets: Reactants are usually two aqueous solutions containing soluble ions, e.g., BaCl2(aq) + CuSO4(aq).
Products include an insoluble solid precipitate marked with (s) and another soluble salt marked with (aq).
Example: Ba2+(aq) + SO4 2-(aq) -> BaSO4(s) represents the classic sulfate test precipitation.

callouts.p: In exam questions, precipitates are always marked with (s) in the balanced symbol equation, which is your main clue for writing the net ionic equation.

core.h: Common Pitfalls in Exam Equation Writing
core.p: Examiners routinely penalize candidates for basic errors in formulae transcription and equation balancing. Avoiding these guarantees high marks.
bullets: Failing to write diatomic gases correctly (writing O instead of O2).
Altering subscript numbers inside formulae instead of using stoichiometric coefficients.
Omitting state symbols when specifically demanded by the command word.
Incorrectly balancing polyatomic ion groups by changing internal oxygen numbers.

callouts.p: Always double check atom counts before moving on. Left side atoms must equal right side atoms for every single element.

analogy.t: The Recipe and Kitchen Ingredients Analogy
analogy.p: Writing chemical formulae and balancing equations is like following a recipe in a professional kitchen. Each chemical formula is like a specific ingredient card (e.g., 2 hydrogen atoms bonded to 1 oxygen atom for water). Balancing an equation is like scaling a recipe so that nothing is wasted: if you have 4 burger buns (reactants), you must have 4 burger patties (products) so no food is left over or magically generated. Where the analogy breaks down is that chemical reactions transform substances into entirely new chemical entities with different properties, whereas cooking is mostly physical and chemical mixing without nuclear transmutation.

terms.d: A combination of symbols showing the exact ratio and types of atoms in a substance.
A positively charged ion formed by the loss of electrons.
A negatively charged ion formed by the gain of electrons.
An ion containing more than one atom covalently bonded together with an overall charge.
A technique using ion charges to determine the empirical formula of an ionic compound.
An equation representing a reaction with equal numbers of each atom on both sides.
The large number placed in front of a formula in an equation to balance atom counts.
Letters (s, l, g, aq) indicating the physical state of reactants and products.
Describes a substance dissolved in water.
An ion that does not take part in a chemical reaction and remains unchanged in solution.
An equation that highlights reacting ions in solution while omitting spectator ions.
An equation showing the loss or gain of electrons by ions during electrolysis or redox.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions react together.
The scientific law stating that matter is neither created nor destroyed during a chemical reaction.

mistakes.w: Writing oxygen gas as O in a reaction equation
mistakes.r: Oxygen is diatomic and must always be written as O2

mistakes.w: Changing the formula of magnesium oxide from MgO to MgO2 to balance oxygen
mistakes.r: Never change internal subscripts; use stoichiometric coefficients like 2MgO instead

mistakes.w: Writing the formula of calcium nitrate as CaN2O6
mistakes.r: Use brackets for polyatomic ions: Ca(NO3)2

mistakes.w: Omitting state symbols when the question specifically asks for them
mistakes.r: Always include (s), (l), (g), and (aq) if state symbols are requested in the command words

mistakes.w: Splitting insoluble solids into ions in ionic equations
mistakes.r: Only aqueous ionic substances are split into ions; solids, liquids, and gases remain intact

mistakes.w: Writing sodium ion charge as Na-
mistakes.r: Sodium is in Group 1 and forms a positive cation: Na+

mistakes.w: Treating sulfate as SO3 instead of SO4
mistakes.r: Memorise common ion formulae precisely: sulfate is SO4 2-

exam.q: Give the chemical formula for aluminium chloride.
exam.tip: Use the cross-over method: Al is 3+, Cl is 1-, cross the numbers to get AlCl3.

exam.q: Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid to produce magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas.
model: Correct reactants and products formulae: Mg + HCl -> MgCl2 + H2 (1)
Correct balancing coefficient 2 in front of HCl (1)
Correct state symbols: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> MgCl2(aq) + H2(g) (1)
exam.tip: Check hydrogen is balanced with 2 on both sides and remember hydrogen is diatomic (H2).

exam.q: State the formula of the ammonium ion.
exam.tip: Ammonium is a rare positive polyatomic ion. Do not confuse with ammonia (NH3).

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide solution.
exam.tip: Neutralisation in aqueous solution is always the reaction of hydrogen ions with hydroxide ions to form water.

exam.q: Balance the following equation: Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3
model: Correct coefficients to balance iron and oxygen: 4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3 (1)
exam.tip: Balance oxygen first by finding the lowest common multiple of 2 and 3, which is 6.

exam.q: Explain what the state symbol (aq) means in a chemical equation.
exam.tip: Do not just write 'in water'; use the exact term 'dissolved in water' or 'aqueous'.

exam.q: Derive the formula for calcium hydroxide using ion charges.
exam.tip: Because hydroxide has a 1- charge and calcium has 2+, you need two hydroxide ions, hence the brackets.

exam.q: Write a half equation for the reduction of copper(II) ions during electrolysis.
exam.tip: Reduction is gain of electrons, so electrons must be on the left-hand side of the half equation.

exam.q: Give the balanced symbol equation, including state symbols, for the reaction of solid calcium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid.
exam.tip: Acid + carbonate produces salt, water, and carbon dioxide gas.

worked.q: Derive the chemical formula for iron(III) sulfate.
steps: Identify the symbols and charges of the ions: Iron(III) is Fe3+ and sulfate is SO4 2-.
Apply the cross-over method: the 3 charge of iron becomes the subscript of sulfate, and the 2 charge of sulfate becomes the subscript of iron.
Since sulfate is a polyatomic ion, enclose it in brackets before applying the subscript.

worked.q: Balance the equation for the combustion of propane: C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O
steps: Count carbon atoms: There are 3 carbons on the left, so put a 4 in front of CO2? No, put a 3 in front of CO2: C3H8 + O2 -> 3CO2 + H2O.
Count hydrogen atoms: There are 8 hydrogens on the left, so put a 4 in front of H2O to give 8 hydrogens: C3H8 + O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O.
Count oxygen atoms on the right: 3 x 2 (from CO2) = 6 oxygens, and 4 x 1 (from H2O) = 4 oxygens. Total = 10 oxygen atoms.
Balance oxygen on the left: Since O2 has 2 oxygen atoms, put a 5 in front of O2 (5 x 2 = 10). Final equation: C3H8(g) + 5O2(g) -> 3CO2(g) + 4H2O(l).

chem_ocrb.1.9.summary: This topic covers the physical and chemical properties of transition metals, which are located in the central block of the Periodic Table between Groups 2 and 3. Compared to Group 1 alkali metals, transition metals have higher melting points, greater densities, and much lower reactivity, while also forming coloured compounds and acting as catalysts. At a Grade 9 level, you must be able to explain their variable oxidation states in compounds and describe their unique catalytic roles in industrial processes such as the Haber and Contact processes.

core.h: Position and Basic Definition of Transition Metals
core.p: Transition metals occupy the large central block of the Periodic Table, situated between Group 2 and Group 3. They are metallic elements that share characteristic physical properties which set them apart from both the reactive alkali metals and main group elements.
bullets: Located in the central block between Group 2 and Group 3.
Include common structural and precious metals like iron, copper, chromium, nickel, and gold.
They are all dense, lustrous solids at room temperature (except mercury, which is a liquid).
Form a bridge between the highly reactive metals on the left and non-metals on the right.

callouts.p: A d-block element that forms one or more stable ions with incompletely filled d orbitals.
Always remember they sit between Group 2 and Group 3, spanning periods 4, 5, and 6.

core.h: Comparison: Transition Metals vs Group 1 Alkali Metals
core.p: While both groups are metallic, transition metals and Group 1 alkali metals have vastly different physical and chemical properties. Group 1 metals are soft, low-density, and extremely reactive, whereas transition metals are hard, strong, dense, and unreactive.
bullets: Transition metals have much higher melting and boiling points than Group 1 metals.
Transition metals are significantly denser and harder; iron can be used for buildings, whereas sodium can be cut with a knife.
Transition metals react very slowly, if at all, with cold water or oxygen at room temperature, unlike Group 1 metals.
Group 1 metals only ever form +1 ions, whereas transition metals can form ions with different charges.

head: Property
Transition Metals (e.g., Iron)
Group 1 Metals (e.g., Sodium)
rows: Soft, easily cut with a scalpel
Very low or none at room temp

callouts.p: Do not say transition metals don't melt; they just melt at much higher temperatures than Group 1.

core.h: Physical Properties: High Density and Mechanical Strength
core.p: Transition metals are prized for their structural applications because of their high mechanical strength, hardness, and high density. These properties arise from strong metallic bonding involving inner d-electrons alongside outer s-electrons.
bullets: High density means atoms are tightly packed together in the metallic lattice.
High tensile strength allows them to support massive loads without breaking or snapping.
Malleable and ductile: they can be hammered into sheets or drawn into wires.
Used extensively in construction (bridges, rebar, structural steel beams).

callouts.p: Iron and its alloys (steel) are the backbone of modern engineering due to strength and abundance.

core.h: Low Chemical Reactivity
core.p: Unlike Group 1 elements, which react violently with air and water, transition metals have very low reactivity. This makes them resistant to corrosion and suitable for long-lasting everyday items and plumbing.
bullets: Do not react vigorously with cold water.
React very slowly with oxygen in the air (some form a protective oxide layer, like chromium and aluminium, though aluminium is technically group 3, stainless steel contains Cr).
Copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid because it is less reactive than hydrogen.
Iron rusts only in the simultaneous presence of oxygen and water over an extended period.

callouts.p: Always state transition metals are 'less reactive than Group 1 metals' rather than 'unreactive'.

core.h: Variable Oxidation States and Ion Charges
core.p: A defining chemical characteristic of transition metals is their ability to form compounds with different positive charges (oxidation states). For example, iron can form iron(II) with Fe2+ ions and iron(III) with Fe3+ ions.
bullets: Group 1 metals only form +1 ions, and Group 2 only form +2 ions. Transition metals have multiple stable ion forms.
Iron forms Fe2+ (pale green solutions usually) and Fe3+ (orange/brown solutions).
Copper forms Cu+ and Cu2+ (blue solutions).
Roman numerals in IUPAC names (e.g., copper(II) sulfate) indicate the specific charge on the metal ion.

callouts.p: The ability of an element to form ions or compounds where the metal has different positive charges.

core.h: Coloured Compounds
core.p: Transition metal compounds are strikingly colourful. Different compounds of the same metal, or compounds of different transition metals, display a wide spectrum of colours depending on the metal's oxidation state and the attached ions.
bullets: Copper(II) sulfate crystals and solutions are bright blue.
Nickel(II) chloride solutions are typically green.
Iron(II) compounds are often pale green, while iron(III) compounds are brown or yellow.
Potassium manganate(VII) is a deep purple solution.
Chromium compounds exhibit colours ranging from green to orange and yellow.

callouts.p: Colour changes are often used in titrations and qualitative analysis to spot the end of a reaction.

core.h: Catalytic Properties of Transition Metals and Their Compounds
core.p: Transition metals and their compounds are exceptionally useful as catalysts. A catalyst speeds up a chemical rate without being used up itself, by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
bullets: Iron is used as a catalyst in the Haber process to manufacture ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
Nickel is used as a catalyst to hydrogenate vegetable oils to make margarine.
Platinum, palladium, and rhodium are used in car catalytic converters to turn toxic gases into harmless ones.
Manganese(IV) oxide catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

callouts.p: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being chemically changed or used up at the end of the reaction.

core.h: Industrial Example 1: Iron in the Haber Process
core.p: The Haber process is used to produce ammonia (NH3) for fertilisers. Finely divided iron is used as a solid heterogeneous catalyst to speed up the reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen gases.
bullets: Equation: N2 (g) + 3H2 (g) <=> 2NH3 (g) (with iron catalyst).
Operates at around 450 °C and 200 atmospheres.
The iron catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium, but helps the system reach equilibrium much faster.
Iron is used in porous, finely divided form to maximise surface area.

callouts.p: Always specify 'iron' or 'finely divided iron' when asked for the Haber process catalyst.

core.h: Industrial Example 2: Nickel in Hydrogenation
core.p: Nickel is the classic catalyst used in the food industry to hydrogenate liquid vegetable oils, turning unsaturated double bonds into single bonds and converting oils into solid spreads like margarine at room temperature.
bullets: Adds hydrogen gas across carbon-carbon double bonds in unsaturated plant oils.
Carried out at elevated temperatures and pressures with a nickel catalyst.
Allows liquid fats to be converted into spreadable fats for culinary use.

callouts.p: Nickel catalyst + hydrogen + vegetable oil = margarine.

core.h: Industrial Example 3: Catalytic Converters in Cars
core.p: Transition metals such as platinum, palladium, and rhodium are coated onto a ceramic honeycomb inside car exhaust systems to reduce toxic emissions before they escape into the atmosphere.
bullets: Converts toxic carbon monoxide (CO) into carbon dioxide (CO2).
Converts unburnt hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide and water.
Reduces toxic nitrogen oxides (NOx) into harmless nitrogen gas (N2) and oxygen gas (O2).
High surface area honeycomb structure maximises contact between exhaust gases and the precious metal catalysts.

callouts.p: Make sure you know the three main pollutants removed: CO, hydrocarbons, and NOx.

analogy.p: Think of Group 1 metals as a cheap, single-use plastic knife: extremely sharp and dangerous when it touches water, but weak and easily bent. Transition metals are like a high-grade stainless steel Swiss Army knife: hard, strong, reliable, able to take on many different tools and forms (variable oxidation states), and useful in countless specialised jobs (catalysts).

terms.d: An element in the d-block of the Periodic Table that forms stable ions with incomplete d orbitals.
A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up.
The ability of an element to form compounds with different positive ionic charges.
Industrial manufacture of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen using an iron catalyst.
Addition of hydrogen across double bonds, catalysed by nickel to harden oils.
Exhaust device using platinum/rhodium/palladium to convert toxic gases into harmless ones.
The resistance of a material to breaking under tension.
Mass per unit volume of a substance.
An iron ion with a charge of +2 (Fe2+).
An iron ion with a charge of +3 (Fe3+).
A transition metal salt that forms characteristic blue solutions in water.
Group 1 element; soft, low density, highly reactive with water (used for contrast).

mistakes.w: Transition metals are extremely reactive like Group 1.
mistakes.r: Transition metals have very low reactivity compared to Group 1 metals.

mistakes.w: Transition metals only form one type of ion.
mistakes.r: Transition metals form variable oxidation states and multiple different positive ions.

mistakes.w: All transition metal compounds are white.
mistakes.r: Transition metal compounds are typically brightly coloured.

mistakes.w: Catalysts get used up during a chemical reaction.
mistakes.r: Catalysts remain chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.

mistakes.w: Transition metals are soft and float on water.
mistakes.r: Transition metals are hard, dense, strong, and sink in water.

mistakes.w: Nickel is used as the catalyst in the Haber process.
mistakes.r: Iron is used as the catalyst in the Haber process; nickel is used for hydrogenation of oils.

mistakes.w: Transition metals melt at room temperature.
mistakes.r: All transition metals (except mercury) are high-melting-point solids at room temperature.

exam.q: Give two physical properties of transition metals that distinguish them from Group 1 metals.
exam.tip: State clear physical comparisons. Do not mention reactivity here as it is chemical.

exam.q: Explain why transition metals are widely used as structural materials compared to Group 1 metals.
model: Transition metals have high tensile strength and are hard / strong
Group 1 metals are very soft and weak
exam.tip: Link the property directly to structural suitability.

exam.q: Name the catalyst used in the industrial manufacture of ammonia via the Haber process.
exam.tip: A one-word answer is often enough, but writing 'iron' or 'finely divided iron' is safest.

exam.q: State two chemical properties that are characteristic of transition metals but not of Group 1 metals.
model: They act as catalysts / they have variable oxidation states
exam.tip: Pick any two of: coloured compounds, variable ion charges/oxidation states, catalytic activity.

exam.q: A student adds copper(II) sulfate solution to a test tube. Describe the appearance of this solution.
exam.tip: Remember that copper(II) solutions are characteristically blue.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by a catalyst in terms of chemical reactions.
model: Remains chemically unchanged / not used up at the end
exam.tip: Both points are required for full marks.

exam.q: State the transition metal used as a catalyst in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils.
exam.tip: Do not confuse nickel (hydrogenation) with iron (Haber process).

exam.q: Give the formula of an iron(III) ion.
exam.tip: Include the charge and the plus sign correctly.

exam.q: Describe how transition metals differ from Group 1 metals in their reaction with water at room temperature.
model: Group 1 metals react vigorously / violently with water
Transition metals do not react with cold water or react extremely slowly

exam.q: Explain why catalytic converters contain transition metals such as platinum and rhodium in a honeycomb structure.
model: They act as catalysts to convert toxic gases into harmless gases
Honeycomb structure provides a large surface area
exam.tip: Mention both the catalytic action and the high surface area design.

worked.q: Compare the properties of potassium (Group 1) and iron (Transition metal) under three different headings: melting point, density, and ion formation.
steps: Melting point: Potassium is low (~63 °C); Iron is high (~1538 °C).
Density: Potassium is low (floats on oil/water); Iron is high (sinks, dense).
Ion formation: Potassium forms only +1 ions (K+); Iron forms variable oxidation states like Fe2+ and Fe3+.
worked.ans: Potassium has a low melting point, low density, and forms only +1 ions. Iron has a high melting point, high density, and forms variable positive ions (Fe2+, Fe3+).

worked.q: Identify the transition metal catalyst used in: (a) The Haber process, (b) Hydrogenation of oils, (c) Car exhaust catalytic converters.
steps: (c) Car exhaust catalytic converters: Platinum, palladium, or rhodium.
